title: How to Get Your Security Deposit Back
description: How to get your security deposit back: what to do on move-in day, what landlords can charge, a letter to copy, deadlines and what to do if they refuse.

cover.alt: A set of keys on an envelope next to a small camera

keywords: how to get security deposit back security deposit deductions wear and tear deposit letter landlord
takeaways: Your deposit is won or lost on move-in day: photograph everything and send the landlord your notes.
Landlords can charge for damage, not normal wear and tear.
Ask in writing, with your photos. Most states set a deadline for returning the deposit.
body:
Your security deposit is your money. Your landlord holds it as a safety net, not as a bonus they get to keep at the end. Yet plenty of renters never see the full amount again, and rarely because they wrecked the place. Money disappears over small things: a cleaning charge nobody can explain, a scuffed wall that was already scuffed on day one, a deadline that quietly passed.

Getting it back is mostly a paperwork game, and paperwork is a game you can win. This guide walks through the whole job in order: what to do on move-in day, what counts as normal wear and tear, how to clean and hand the place back, the letter to send if your money is late, and what to do if your landlord keeps money that is not theirs.

## Your deposit is won or lost on move-in day

Most people start thinking about their deposit in the last week of the lease. By then, the most useful evidence is a year old and nobody took it. Renters who get the full amount back almost always did one boring thing at the start: they recorded the home's condition before unpacking.

Walk through every room with your phone before your furniture goes in. Take wide photos, then close-ups of anything already worn: marks on walls, stains on carpet, chips in the sink, a cracked tile. Run the taps and flush the toilet. Then write a condition list, room by room, and email it with the photos to your landlord or agent the same day. An emailed list carries a date, and a dated record is hard to argue with twelve months later.

Keep everything in one folder: your signed lease, deposit receipt, proof of rent payments, and that condition list. [First apartment costs](/blog/first-apartment-costs/) covers what moving in really costs.

| Area               | What to photograph and note                |
|--------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| Walls and ceilings | Marks, holes, cracks, damp, paint color    |
| Floors and carpets | Stains, burns, scratches, worn patches     |
| Kitchen            | Oven working, fridge seals, counter chips  |
| Bathroom           | Tiles, grout, sealant, drips, toilet flush |
| Windows and doors  | Locks, cracked glass, keys given           |
| Meter readings     | Electric, gas, water readings              |

One more move-in job: find out where your deposit sits. In England and Wales, your landlord must place it in a government-approved protection scheme within 30 days and tell you which one. In New South Wales in Australia, the bond is lodged with NSW Fair Trading, a government body, not your landlord's account. Ask for the paperwork.

### Move-in day checklist

Work through this on moving day, before the boxes take over. Print it or copy it into your notes app.

- Take dated photos of every room before any furniture goes in: floors, walls and windows.
- Photograph existing marks, stains or damage up close, with something in the frame for scale.
- Read the electricity, gas and water meters and photograph each reading.
- Put the readings, the date and the supplier names in one note and email it to yourself.
- Test every tap, light switch, socket and appliance, and list anything that does not work.
- Check that windows and doors lock properly.
- Write down the condition of carpets, curtains and blinds, room by room.
- Collect the documents: signed lease, inventory, deposit receipt or protection details, and the landlord's contact details.
- Send the landlord your condition notes and photos in writing within the first few days.
- Agree how shared bills get split and paid if you live with others.

## What your landlord can and cannot charge you for

In most places, allowed deductions form a short list. The Legal Aid Center of Southern Nevada sums it up in three items, and the same pattern shows up in many states and countries: unpaid rent, reasonable cleaning costs, and damage beyond normal wear and tear. Some leases also allow unpaid utility bills you owed.

So most arguments come down to one question: is this wear and tear, or is it damage? Wear and tear is what happens when a home is simply lived in. Paint fades. Carpet flattens where people walk. Tiny nail holes appear where pictures hung. That is the landlord's cost of doing business. Damage is something you broke, stained, or changed without permission.

| Wear and tear (landlord pays)  | Damage (comes from your deposit) |
|--------------------------------|----------------------------------|
| Paint faded or lightly scuffed | Large holes in walls or doors    |
| Carpet worn in walkways        | Burns, stains, tears in carpet   |
| Small nail holes from pictures | Broken blinds or fixtures        |
| Loose hinges, worn finish      | Pet damage or smoke smell        |
| Slight limescale               | Walls repainted unapproved       |

Watch out for vague charges. A line that says “cleaning fee” with a round number and no detail is worth questioning. In many places the landlord has to itemize deductions, listing each charge and its cost. If a figure looks invented, ask for the invoice.

## Move-out cleaning: leave it as you found it

The standard in most leases is simple: hand the place back in the same condition as move-in, allowing for normal wear and tear. It does not have to look brand new. It does have to be properly clean. Work through this list once the furniture is out, because dirt hides behind sofas.

- Kitchen: clean the oven and stove, wipe grease off tiles and cupboard fronts, empty and clean the fridge.
- Bathroom: scrub tiles and grout, clear limescale from taps and shower head, clean mirrors, empty cabinets.
- Floors: vacuum everywhere, mop hard floors, spot-clean marks on carpets.
- Walls: wipe off scuffs and fingerprints. Fill small holes only if your lease asks.
- Every room: take all your belongings out, including attics, sheds, and garages. Landlords can charge for removing items left behind.

When you finish, photograph every room again, empty and clean, plus the meter readings. Paired with your move-in photos, they settle most arguments before they start.

## The quiet admin steps that protect you

Three small tasks in your final week make a real difference. First, give your landlord a forwarding address in writing. Email is fine; keep a copy. In some places the landlord's duty to return your money, and sometimes the deadline itself, only starts once they have an address to send it to. Second, return every key, fob, and remote, and ask for a receipt or photograph the handover. A lost-key charge for a full lock change is a classic deduction. Third, ask for a joint final walkthrough, checklist in hand.

## What a fair refund looks like

Here is an illustration with made-up numbers. Say your rent is $1,000 a month and your deposit is $1,000. You move out on time, owing no rent. Your landlord deducts $120 for cleaning the oven and carpets, left greasy and marked, and $80 to replace a blind you broke. Total deductions: $200. Your refund: $800.

Now change one detail. The landlord instead charges $400 to repaint the whole apartment because the paint looks tired. Faded paint from everyday living is wear and tear in most places, so challenge that in writing, with your move-in photos attached. The difference is evidence.

## Copy and paste: the letter asking for your deposit back

If your local deadline has passed, or it is close, send a short, polite letter. Polite and written beats angry and phoned, because a letter creates a record. Fill in the brackets and send by email, and by tracked mail too for proof of delivery.

Dear [landlord or agent name],

I moved out of [property address] on [move-out date] and returned all keys the same day. My security deposit was $[amount], paid on [date paid].

Please return my deposit, minus any lawful deductions, to [bank details or address]. If you are keeping any part of it, please send an itemized list showing each deduction and its cost.

My forwarding address is [your new address]. You can reach me at [email] or [phone number].

Thank you,

[Your full name]

### If that gets ignored: the firmer follow-up

Give the first letter a fair chance, then send this one, which names the rule, the date, and your next step.

Dear [landlord or agent name],

I am writing again about my security deposit of $[amount] for [property address]. I moved out on [date] and wrote to you on [date of first letter]. Under the rules in [your state, province, or country], my deposit or an itemized list of deductions was due by [deadline date]. That date has passed.

Please return the full $[amount] by [date, giving 7 to 14 days]. If I do not receive it, I will take the next step open to me: [the free dispute service of my deposit scheme / a tribunal application / a claim in small claims court], and ask for any extra amount the law allows.

[Your full name]

## How long can they take? Deadlines where you live

There is no single worldwide deadline, and anyone who gives you one number for every country is guessing. Canada, for example, sets its rules province by province. Here is the honest picture.

United States. Each state sets its own deadline, usually a few weeks after you move out. Nevada, for example, gives a landlord no later than 30 days after the tenancy ends to return the deposit or hand over an itemized list of deductions, according to the Legal Aid Center of Southern Nevada. If a court there finds a landlord wrongfully kept the money, it can order them to pay up to twice the deposit amount on top. Other states differ, so check your state's housing or attorney general pages, or ask a local legal aid office.

United Kingdom. The system does much of the chasing for you. Because your deposit sits in an approved protection scheme, your landlord must return it within 10 days of you both agreeing how much you get back, GOV.UK says. If you cannot agree, the scheme holds the money while its free dispute resolution service reviews the evidence. If your landlord never protected the deposit at all, a county court can order it repaid plus compensation of up to three times the deposit.

Australia. Your bond is held by a state authority, not your landlord. In New South Wales, you claim it through Rental Bonds Online or on a paper form. NSW Fair Trading notifies your landlord or agent, who has 14 days to dispute your claim. No dispute, and Fair Trading pays the money into your bank account. If they do dispute it, the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal, NCAT, decides the split. Other states run similar systems.

## When money is wrongly kept: what to do, in order

If your refund arrives short, or does not arrive at all, work through these steps in order. Most disputes end at step two or three.

1. Ask for the deductions in writing, itemized. You cannot argue with a charge you cannot see.
2. Lay your evidence beside each charge: move-in photos, the emailed condition list, rent receipts, move-out photos.
3. Reply in writing, charge by charge. Agree with anything fair, say why the rest is not, attach photos, and name the amount you expect back.
4. Use the free route where one exists: the dispute service of your UK deposit scheme, a tribunal application in Australia, or free tenant advice and legal aid in the US.
5. If you have not already, send the firmer letter above with a clear final date.
6. As a last step, file a claim. In the US that usually means small claims court, built for sums like a deposit, with no lawyer required. Some places let the court award extra when a deposit was kept in bad faith.

Keep every message in writing. Nobody can show a judge a phone call. And while the argument runs, start rebuilding money for your next place: [sinking funds for beginners](/blog/sinking-funds-for-beginners/) shows how to save a deposit in small monthly pieces.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can my landlord keep my whole deposit for cleaning?

Only if the cleaning bill genuinely comes to that much, which is rare for a home left in decent shape. Deductions should cover bringing the place back to its move-in standard, at a real cost, ideally with invoices. A huge round figure with no breakdown is worth disputing.

### What counts as normal wear and tear?

The wear from normal living: faded paint, light scuffs, carpet flattened in walkways, small picture-hook holes, fittings loosened by everyday use. Damage is the opposite: broken, stained, burned, or changed by you or your guests.

### I shared the deposit with roommates. How do we split the refund?

Agree the split in writing before anyone moves out, based on who caused any damage and who paid what in. [How to split bills with roommates](/blog/how-to-split-bills-with-roommates/) covers fair ways to divide shared housing costs. The refund often goes to the names on the lease or bond, so sort the split early.

### My landlord never protected my deposit. What then?

In England and Wales this is a serious breach. GOV.UK explains that you can apply to your local county court, which can order the deposit repaid and up to three times the deposit amount on top. Citizens Advice or Shelter can advise you first.

### I did break something. Can they charge me full replacement cost?

They can charge for the damage, but you can question a brand-new price for an old item. A five-year-old carpet was not worth its original price the day you damaged it. Ask how the figure was worked out, plus the item's age and condition. Fair charges reflect remaining value.

One last thought: if you are renewing rather than moving, your deposit simply rolls on, and the money conversation worth having is about next year's rent. [How to negotiate rent](/blog/negotiate-your-rent/) walks through that discussion. Either way, treat the paperwork like it matters, because it does.

## A quick note

This article is general information only, based on the sources below, and it is not legal or financial advice. Rules, deadlines, and penalties differ by state, province, and country, and they change. For your situation, check your local tenancy authority or a legal aid service.
